content:
President Trump caused alarm among some observers on Monday when he spoke about the Iran war at a midterm campaign rally in Grand Island, Nebraska, saying the cost of the war was "slightly high" but ultimately just a "very small price" — and then appeared to suggest Iran could strike two major California cities.

"It's a very small price to pay for keeping the world safe, and keeping our country safe. They could destroy a city — let them destroy Los Angeles, let them destroy San Diego," he said. "It's a very small price, and the war will be over very soon. Actually, it's almost over. They might drag it out a little bit longer, you know, they always say they have a high tolerance for pain; they have to do that. I tell you, they have to do that. But it'll be over very soon."

When reporters asked Trump on Tuesday to clarify what he meant by "let them destroy Los Angeles, let them destroy San Diego," Trump appeared to brush off the question.

The crowd cheered when Trump mentioned Iran "destroying" the two cities. The event was a campaign stop for Republican Nebraska Senator Pete Ricketts.

The U.S. and Israel launched coordinated missile attacks on Iran on Feb. 28, kicking off a war that has stretched on for months. The president has claimed the war in Iran is necessary to prevent Iran from developing nuclear weapons and to protect Israel, according to HuffPost.

California Governor Gavin Newsom posted on X on Tuesday morning, calling the remarks "dangerous — and potentially treasonous." He wrote: "That's tantamount to putting a target on our two largest cities, and one of America's largest military ports. I've directed the state Threat Assessment Center to actively monitor the situation in case foreign actors interpret the president's words as an invitation to attack California."

San Diego Mayor Todd Gloria said in an official statement: "President Trump should retract these comments and apologize to the people of San Diego. The president has no right to decide which American communities deserve protection."

Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass posted on X, calling the president's remarks "dangerous" and saying the president should focus on protecting Americans, not encouraging attacks on American cities.

The White House directed HuffPost to White House communications director Steven Cheung's X post, in which he said Trump "made it clear that without stopping a nuclear-armed Iran, U.S. cities would be threatened. America is safer because of this president. Iran has no nuclear weapons, no navy, no air force, and no money."

As of publication, Trump had not publicly clarified his remarks. Ricketts' office had not responded to HuffPost's request for comment by the time of publication.

Luke Winslow, a rhetoric professor in Baylor University's communication department, told HuffPost that this kind of language is unprecedented compared to past presidents' war remarks.

"Generally speaking, wartime presidential rhetoric aims to unite the country, not divide it. At the same time, in a sense, this is consistent with the unprecedented nature of Trump as a president," Winslow noted.

Winslow said Trump has shown a high regard for loyalty tests throughout his two terms, and that ahead of the midterms, he wanted to rally the crowd in attendance.

"The content of what he says is designed to generate excitement and attention. Most people would agree that his political genius is his ability to capture attention and manipulate the news cycle — we've seen that for a decade. What he does is say things he knows will become headlines or get the crowd excited," Winslow said.

Robert Rowland, a University of Kansas communications professor, also pointed out that the crowd's response became an enabler and affirmation for the president.

"Why would anyone laugh at the idea of Los Angeles or San Diego potentially being attacked?" Rowland asked. He continued: "People aren't laughing at the idea of a real physical attack. Their laughter reflects their dissatisfaction with the coastal elite."

Rowland said that unlike past presidents, Trump also specifically targets individual groups, as well as his personal grudges against certain specific groups in America.

"The most rhetorically skilled presidents [Reagan and Obama] focused on what people have in common. Historically, rhetoric that portrays certain groups as not 'truly' American, as 'other,' has the potential to inspire extremist organizations. At the same time, this kind of rhetoric can also indirectly contribute to political violence," he said.

Did Trump commit treason?

Newsom's post raised one possibility: that Trump's remarks could be described as "treasonous." Treason is a legal term defined in the Constitution as "levying War against [the United States], or in adhering to their Enemies, giving them Aid and Comfort. No Person shall be convicted of Treason unless on the Testimony of two Witnesses to the same overt Act, or on Confession in open Court."

However, legal experts who spoke with HuffPost said Trump's words do not amount to treason, because treason has a very precise definition.

Greg Magarian, a law professor at Washington University in St. Louis, told HuffPost: "The Constitution's understanding of treason is very narrow; it only covers levying war against the United States, or providing aid and comfort to the enemies of the United States, and in this case, whatever you think of Trump ... he was saying this in the context of talking about how to win this war."

Magarian added: "There's no indication that he's surrendering, or that he's helping the other side, or that he wants to give Iran a blueprint for bombing Los Angeles. So this is not even close to [treason]."

Cheung's statement argued that Trump was describing what could have happened if the U.S. had not stopped Iran, rather than saying Iran should attack Los Angeles and San Diego. Carlton Larson, a law professor at UC Davis School of Law, told HuffPost that if it were the latter, it might constitute Trump levying war, but treason would still require the use of force and providing aid to Iran.

Larson noted: "All the levying war cases require an actual use of force, and Trump here is just giving a speech. The cases [also] require actual aid and comfort to the enemy, and this rambling speech would likely not qualify as genuine aid and comfort."
